topic: distributed consensus; stability; memory; stochastic versus worst-case evaluation
status: bounded synthesis of one sampled 2011 full text and a targeted 2008 full-text counterexample
claim: For the audited binary long-lived-consensus models, worst-case geodesic output flips and random-walk average flips are distinct objectives and can rank rules differently; one bit of memory changes the average-stability optimum. A stability claim must name its path distribution, fault model and memory allowance.
positive_evidence: The 2011 sampled paper defines worst-case instability over geodesic paths and states inst(n,t)=2t+1 as a conjecture; its general theorem proves the equality only for t=0 and t=1, plus selected parameter cases.
The 2008 full-text follow-up gives a binary t=0 example where a geodesic-optimal memoryless rule has random-walk average instability 1/n, while an average-optimal memoryless rule can have n/2^n.
The 2008 paper constructs a one-bit-memory rule attaining its stated average optimum.
counterevidence: The 2011 paper’s lower bounds and constructions can coincide for selected parameters, and its full general conjecture may have been addressed by later literature not established by this audit.
Both sources use formal binary input models; neither validates workload-weighted stability on a live sensor or distributed-service trace.

sources.title: Average Binary Long-Lived Consensus: Quantifying the Stabilizing Role Played by Memory
sources.sections: Geodesic/average instability definitions; memoryless counterexample; one-bit memory theorem

falsifiable_test: On preregistered binary fault-tolerant consensus instances, compare memoryless and one-bit-memory policies over both exhaustive geodesics and held-out workload/random-walk paths. Report worst-case flips, mean and tail flips, and include path-distribution shifts. The claim weakens if rule rankings and optimum remain invariant across these criteria and memory budgets.
limitations: Only two bounded formal studies were audited; neither uses a deployment trace. This is not a statement about the current resolution status of the 2011 conjecture.

topic: distributed storage; locally repairable codes; repair performance
status: bounded synthesis of two sampled full texts and a targeted 2023 trace-replay follow-up
claim: Repair locality (symbols accessed) is not a sufficient proxy for storage efficiency, repair bandwidth, bytes read, repair latency or practical recoverability. Code parameters and the realized erasure/layout pattern jointly shape operational outcomes.
positive_evidence: The 2012 LRC paper explicitly distinguishes locality from repair bandwidth and bits read, and bounds the locality/distance/storage tradeoff.

The 2013 HDFS-Xorbas prototype reports 41–52% as much repair data read and 25–45% shorter repair duration than HDFS-RS under its tested EC2 failures, at roughly 14% extra storage; its network was not saturated.

A 2023 Google/USENIX FAST trace-replay study reports 0/278 unavailable stripes recovered before restoration by one deployed wide-code configuration versus 92/278 (33%) under a same-width/overhead Uniform Cauchy LRC simulation, demonstrating sensitivity to construction and observed erasure patterns.
counterevidence: Xorbas is an empirical prototype result and did show sizable savings in its tested setup; this finding does not negate those results.
The 2023 92/278 result is counterfactual replay, not a live intervention, and the deployed/replayed constructions and stripe patterns may not represent other fleets.
The 2012 theorem establishes meaningful parameter guarantees; the boundary is that those guarantees do not directly predict all system-level metrics.

sources.sections: Sec. 5: experiment setup, failure pattern, bytes read, network, duration and storage-overhead adjustment

sources.title: Practical Design Considerations for Wide Locally Recoverable Codes (LRCs)
sources.sections: Cluster stripe replay; Uniform Cauchy LRC results; group-layout discussion

falsifiable_test: Replay multi-cluster correlated-failure and maintenance traces across code families at matched durability, storage overhead, stripe width and placement. Measure recoverability before restoration, symbol accesses, actual bytes read/network bytes, degraded-read latency and repair completion time; follow with a staged randomized deployment if feasible. The claim weakens if locality alone predicts these outcomes after matching design and trace covariates.
limitations: Three papers span distinct code models and generations; results are not directly comparable. One prototype has a small failure schedule and an unsaturated network, and the later operational comparison is counterfactual replay rather than a live intervention.

topic: distributed storage; erasure coding; repair I/O and reliability
status: falsifiable follow-up proposal grounded in one sampled HDFS prototype study and one newer trace-replay study
claim: Reported repair-I/O and latency gains for a locally repairable code should be re-tested with storage overhead and failure exposure included; an unsaturated small-cluster result alone does not establish the gain under production network saturation or correlated failures.
positive_evidence: Xorbas reports lower repair bytes and duration than RS in three progressively larger EC2 file-count trials and a Facebook test cluster.
The Xorbas paper estimates its 14% storage overhead causes 14.3% more blocks to be exposed to random failure, a correction that can be incorporated in the comparison.
Later wide-LRC trace replay finds recovery outcomes sensitive to the actual erasure pattern and code/group design.
counterevidence: The Xorbas savings persisted across the reported 50/100/200-file EC2 trials and were also evaluated on a separate Facebook test cluster; the paper argues its storage adjustment does not erase the gains.
This audit does not demonstrate that the gains disappear under correlated failures or saturated links; those are proposed boundary tests.

sources.title: Practical Design Considerations for Wide Locally Recoverable Codes (LRCs)
sources.sections: Operational stripe availability replay and design considerations

falsifiable_test: Compare Xorbas-like LRC and RS at matched data volume and placement under independent and correlated failure/maintenance traces, both below and at network saturation. Predefine durability, block-loss-adjusted I/O, bandwidth, repair latency, degraded-read cost and storage overhead. The concern is resolved for a target workload if LRC gains and durability remain robust across held-out traces and saturated operation.
limitations: A targeted replication question, not evidence that an existing study is defective. The audited results use older Hadoop, small controlled clusters and limited failure schedules.
